title: CXMT Overtakes Tencent as China's Most Valuable Company as AI Memory Boom Reshapes Markets
subhead: Chinese memory chipmaker CXMT has surpassed Tencent by market capitalization, capping a stunning post-IPO run, while Japan Inc. lifts profit forecasts on AI infrastructure demand and Southeast Asia's chip boom pushes Vietnam and the Philippines toward high-income status.

sections.heading: CXMT Becomes China's Most Valuable Company
sections.body: Chinese memory chipmaker CXMT surpassed Tencent Holdings by market capitalization on Thursday, becoming the most valuable company listed on the mainland or in Hong Kong, according to Nikkei Asia. CXMT went public in July and jumped 465% on its debut, briefly topping Intel's market cap, and has since ridden the AI-driven memory crunch to the top of China's equity rankings. The milestone underscores how the global memory shortage — and Beijing's push for domestic chip self-sufficiency — has turned a state-backed DRAM maker into the country's most valuable listed company, displacing the internet giants that long dominated Chinese markets.
sections.whyItMatters: A memory chipmaker, not a platform company, now anchors Chinese equity markets — a direct signal of where Beijing's industrial policy and the AI boom are directing capital.

sections.heading: Japan Inc. Lifts Profit Forecasts on AI and Chip Demand
sections.body: Japan's listed companies now expect net profit to rise 14% for the year ending March 2027, led by suppliers with high market shares in AI-related infrastructure and manufacturing, Nikkei Asia reports. Hitachi expects greater profit from its high global share in power transmission and distribution equipment, which benefits from the data center boom, while component leaders like Ibiden anticipate gains. The upgrade reflects how the AI buildout is flowing through to Japan's industrial base — from power gear to chip substrates — rather than concentrating only in the largest tech names.
sections.whyItMatters: Japan's broad-based profit upgrade shows the AI capex cycle is now a mainstream earnings driver for industrial suppliers, not just a US tech story.

sections.heading: ASEAN Chip Boom Pushes Vietnam, Philippines Toward High-Income Status
sections.body: The growth of the semiconductor industry in Southeast Asia is reconfiguring regional economic development, putting Vietnam and the Philippines on course toward 'high-income country' status, Nikkei Asia reports. Among the 11 ASEAN members, only Singapore and Brunei currently qualify as high-income by World Bank metrics. The chip boom — spanning assembly, testing and packaging as global firms diversify supply chains — is now seen as the key to escaping the middle-income trap for both economies, even as they remain downstream of the design and fabrication centers in the US, Taiwan and China.
sections.whyItMatters: Supply-chain diversification is translating into a structural economic upgrade for Southeast Asia, giving the region a growing stake in the semiconductor order rather than a peripheral role.

sections.heading: Taiwan Think Tank Warns of 'China Shock' in Physical AI and Robotics
sections.body: The world could be headed for another 'China shock' as Beijing mounts a whole-nation effort to dominate next-generation advanced robotics and physical AI, according to a new assessment by Taiwan's DSET think tank, reported by Nikkei Asia. DSET says Beijing is applying a strategy similar to its earlier EV and drone pushes, even though China still lags in cutting-edge chips, sensors and precision machine tools. The warning frames physical AI — embodied systems that perceive and act in the real world — as the next frontier in the US-China tech race, with Beijing betting on scale and state coordination to close the gap.
sections.whyItMatters: If China replicates its EV and drone playbook in robotics, the next competitive battleground shifts from pure compute to embodied AI — where manufacturing scale and supply chains matter as much as model quality.

sections.heading: Ukraine Hits Wildberries in Coordinated Cyber-Kinetic Operation
sections.body: Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR) claimed it disrupted operations at Wildberries, Russia's largest online marketplace, in a cyberattack carried out with the Cyber Corps hacker group, The Record reports. HUR said the attack hit customer service, contact centers and payment infrastructure, amplifying the impact of Ukrainian drone strikes on the company's warehouses. Russian media estimates Wildberries has lost more than 1.2 million square meters of warehouse space to Ukrainian attacks, and Ukraine's Defense Ministry said seven of the company's ten largest logistics centers had been taken out of operation. The claims could not be independently verified, and Wildberries has not publicly commented.
sections.whyItMatters: The operation shows Ukraine deliberately pairing cyber and kinetic strikes against a single commercial target — a model of integrated warfare aimed at a company it says finances Russia's war effort.

sections.heading: Poland Probes Healthcare Breach Affecting Up to 19 Million
sections.body: Polish authorities are investigating a cyberattack on healthcare software provider MyDr that may have exposed data belonging to nearly 19 million people and more than 12,000 medical facilities, The Record reports. Hackers obtained unauthorized access to historical data held in MyDr systems through April 2024, though authorities said it may not involve all customers or patients. As a precaution, Poland's e-Health Center is replacing digital certificates used by medical systems to connect to the P1 national e-health platform, even though no evidence has been found that certificates were stolen or misused. Poland's Personal Data Protection Office plans to inspect MyDr.
sections.whyItMatters: A breach at a single software vendor that connects to a national health platform exposes the concentration risk in digital health infrastructure — one compromised supplier can threaten trust in an entire country's e-health system.

sections.heading: HEO and Planet Expand Non-Earth Imaging for US Government
sections.body: Australian company HEO has signed an agreement to use Planet's SkySat high-resolution satellites for non-Earth imaging (NEI) — taking images of other space objects from space — initially for US government customers, SpaceNews reports. The partnership gives HEO access to more than 50 sensors in orbit across Earth observation constellations it can task to observe other spacecraft. HEO CEO Will Crowe said the approach avoids 'huge, expensive satellites' and instead relies on 'cameras in the right place at the right time,' citing growing commercial interest in detecting and characterizing potentially nefarious activity in space.
sections.whyItMatters: The deal expands the pool of on-orbit sensors available for space domain awareness, giving governments a cheaper, more distributed way to monitor satellites and detect suspicious behavior in orbit.

sections.heading: Japan's Rare Earth Squeeze Deepens as Inventories Drain
sections.body: Japan is finding it increasingly difficult to source rare earths for electric vehicles and chipmaking equipment as Chinese trade restrictions squeeze supplies, with dysprosium and yttrium imports down around 80% compared to two years ago, Nikkei Asia reports. Japanese materials companies are drawing down rare-earth inventories to maintain deliveries to major customers. The squeeze, which follows Beijing's export curbs, is forcing Japanese firms to ration scarce heavy rare earths critical to EV motors and semiconductor tools.
sections.whyItMatters: With inventories being consumed and no near-term alternative supply, Japan's rare earth exposure is shifting from a cost problem to a potential production constraint for its EV and chip industries.

bottomLine: Today's developments show the AI boom consolidating into hard industrial and market reality: CXMT's rise to China's most valuable company marks the memory crunch as the defining chip story of the year, Japan's broad profit upgrade confirms AI infrastructure demand is now a mainstream earnings driver, and Southeast Asia's chip boom is lifting whole economies. On the security side, Ukraine's coordinated cyber-kinetic strike on Wildberries and Poland's MyDr healthcare breach both underscore how digital infrastructure has become a first-order target — in war and in national health systems alike. The rare earth squeeze on Japan and the DSET warning on Chinese robotics point to the next fronts in the technology-power competition.
sources: Nikkei Asia, The Record (Recorded Future News), SpaceNews
